article.title: GLASS
footer: Adapted from "Glass: Capturing the Dance of Light" by William S. Ellis, National Geographic

items.sentence_raw: Glass, in one form or another, has long been in noble service to humans.

As one of the most widely used of manufactured materials, and certainly the most versatile, it can be as imposing as a telescope mirror with a width of a tennis court or as small and simple as a marble rolling across dirt.

The uses of this adaptable material have been broadened dramatically by new technologies glass fibre optics - more than eight million miles - carrying telephone and television signals across nations, glass ceramics serving as the nose cones of missiles and as crowns for teeth; tiny glass beads taking radiation doses inside the body to specific organs, even a new type of glass fashioned of nuclear waste in order to dispose of that unwanted material.
items.explain:
Q1: The passage lists many specific examples like *'fibre optics'* and *'crowns for teeth'*. These are all **'everyday uses'** of glass in modern life. The heading **'Everyday uses of glass'** matches this list perfectly. So the answer is **viii**.

Q9: The passage lists *'crowns for teeth'* as a current use of glass ceramics. **'Crowns for teeth'** are exactly the same as **'dental fittings'**. Since the text says this happens now, the answer is **A** (**exist today**).

items.sentence_raw: On the horizon are optical computers.
items.explain: Q10: The text says optical computers are *'on the horizon'*. ***'On the horizon' means coming soon, not here yet***. This phrase clearly points to the **future**, not the present. So the answer is **B** (**will exist in the future**).

items.sentence_raw: These could store programs and process information by means of light - pulses from tiny lasers - rather than electrons.
And the pulses would travel over glass fibres, not copper wire.
These machines could function hundreds of times faster than today's electronic computers and hold vastly more information.
Today fibre optics are used to obtain a clearer image of smaller and smaller objects than ever before - even bacterial viruses.
A new generation of optical instruments is emerging that can provide detailed imaging of the inner workings of cells.

It is the surge in fibre optic use and in liquid crystal displays that has set the U.S. glass industry (a 16 billion dollar business employing some 150,000 workers) to building new plants to meet demand.
items.explain: Q2: The text mentions a *'surge in fibre optic use'* causing new factories to open. **'Surge'** means a sudden increase, which connects to **'growth'** in the heading. This shows the market for glass technology is expanding fast. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: But it is not only in technology and commerce that glass has widened its horizons.
The use of glass as art, a tradition spins back at least to Roman times, is also booming.
Nearly everywhere, it seems, men and women are blowing glass and creating works of art.

"I didn't sell a piece of glass until 1975," Dale Chihuly said, smiling, for in the 18 years since the end of the dry spell, he has become one of the most financially successful artists of the 20th century.
He now has a new commission - a glass sculpture for the headquarters building of a pizza company - for which his fee is half a million dollars.
items.explain: Q11: The writer mentions an artist who has a *'new commission'* for a *'glass sculpture'*. A **'commission'** is a paid job happening now, so sculptures exist today. ***Do not think art is only past history***; the text confirms it is current. The answer is **A** (**exist today**).

items.sentence_raw: But not all the glass technology that touches our lives is ultra-modern.
items.explain: Q3: The passage starts by saying *'not all glass technology... is ultra-modern'*. It then describes an old machine from the *'1920s'* for making light bulbs. This refers to a technology from the past, not today. **'Former'** means old or previous, so the answer is **ix**.

items.sentence_raw: Consider the simple light bulb; at the turn of the century most light bulbs were hand blown, and the cost of one was equivalent to half a day's pay for the average worker.
items.explain: Q3: The passage starts by saying *'not all glass technology... is ultra-modern'*. It then describes an old machine from the *'1920s'* for making light bulbs. This refers to a technology from the past, not today. **'Former'** means old or previous, so the answer is **ix**.

items.sentence_raw: In effect, the invention of the ribbon machine by Corning in the 1920s lighted a nation.
The price of a bulb plunged.
Small wonder that the machine has been called one of the great mechanical achievements of all time.
Yet it is very simple: a narrow ribbon of molten glass travels over a moving belt of steel in which there are holes.
items.explain:
Q6: The diagram shows material moving over a belt, and the text says *'a narrow ribbon of molten glass travels'*. **'Molten'** just means melted, so the label must be **'molten glass'**. You can also write **'ribbon of glass'** because both words appear together. The answer is **'molten glass'**.

Q7: The passage states the glass moves over a *'moving belt of steel'*. The diagram points to this metal band underneath the glass. **'Belt of steel'** is the exact phrase describing this part. So the answer is **'belt of steel'**.

items.sentence_raw: The glass sags through the holes and into waiting moulds.
items.explain: Q8: The text explains that the glass sags *'into waiting moulds'*. These containers give the light bulb its shape. The word **'moulds'** fits the diagram label perfectly. So the answer is **'moulds'**.

items.sentence_raw: Puffs of compressed air then shape the glass.
In this way, the envelope of a light bulb is made by a single machine at the rate of 66,000 an hour, as compared with 1,200 a day produced by a team of four glassblowers.
The secret of the versatility of glass lies in its interior structure.
items.explain: Q4: The text explains that the *'secret of the versatility'* lies in the *'interior structure'*. **'Versatility'** means being able to change easily, which is the same as **'adaptable'**. The paragraph tells us exactly what makes glass so flexible. So the answer is **iii**.

items.sentence_raw: Although it is rigid, and thus like a solid, the atoms are arranged in a random disordered fashion, characteristic of a liquid.

In the melting process, the atoms in the raw materials are disturbed from their normal position in the molecular structure; before they can find their way back to crystalline arrangements the glass cools.
This looseness in molecular structure gives the material what engineers call tremendous "formability" which allows technicians to tailor glass to whatever they need.
items.explain: Q4: The text explains that the *'secret of the versatility'* lies in the *'interior structure'*. **'Versatility'** means being able to change easily, which is the same as **'adaptable'**. The paragraph tells us exactly what makes glass so flexible. So the answer is **iii**.

items.sentence_raw: Today, scientists continue to experiment with new glass mixtures and building designers test their imaginations with applications of special types of glass.
A London architect, Mike Davies, sees even more dramatic buildings using molecular chemistry.
items.explain: Q5: An architect talks about using glass as a *'dynamic skin'* for future buildings. He imagines glass that changes color or acts as curtains. This describes testing new ideas for building design. **'Architectural experiments'** matches these creative building tests, so the answer is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: "Glass is the great building material of the future, the 'dynamic skin'," he said.
items.explain: Q5: An architect talks about using glass as a *'dynamic skin'* for future buildings. He imagines glass that changes color or acts as curtains. This describes testing new ideas for building design. **'Architectural experiments'** matches these creative building tests, so the answer is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: "Think of glass that has been treated to react to electric currents going through it, glass that will change from clear to opaque at the push of a button, that gives you instant curtains.
Think of how the tall buildings in New York could perform a symphony of colours as the glass in them is made to change colours instantly."
Glass as instant curtains is available now, but the cost is exorbitant.
items.explain: Q13: The text explicitly states *'Glass as instant curtains is available now'*. **'Available now'** means the same as **'exist today'**. ***Ignore the high cost mentioned later***; availability is what matters here. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: As for the glass changing colours instantly, that may come true.
Mike Davies's vision may indeed be on the way to fulfilment.

orphan_explain_map.12: Q12: The passage discusses glass art, technology, and buildings extensively. However, it never mentions clothing or **'fashions'** at all. ***NOT GIVEN means the information is missing, not false***. Since fashion is absent from the text, the answer is **C**.
